Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Nobody says whether they bet. When the Sofia card comes up, say family pools are normal in many homes and some faiths forbid gambling; nobody’s family is being judged.

Every student in the room

When the Sofia card comes up, say plainly that family pools, card games, and the lottery are normal in many homes and cultures, and that some faiths forbid gambling; nobody's family is being judged.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can work out why parlays and prediction-market contracts favor the app, explain what a prediction market is, and name a few signs that betting is taking up too much room. Nobody is asked whether they bet.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • Index cards for the exit card
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 2 minWhere do you see it?
  2. 4 minThe four-flip parlay
  3. 3 minDo the math: what the app pays
  4. 3 minA bet in a suit and tie, and the Kalshi guess
  5. 2 minWho’s paying for the app? Turn and talk
  6. 4 minFun, or worth a check? Four cards
  7. 2 minEvery family, close

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

The four-flip parlay, the payout guess, and two of the cards.

Before you teach
Let them be the experts.

Some students know odds, spreads, and props far better than most adults. Ask them to explain a parlay or a prop bet to the group. A lecture on the evils of gambling will lose them in a minute; the math lands better when they do it themselves.

Never ask who bets.

Betting is illegal for most of your students and legal for some 18-year-olds on prediction markets. Questions like "Who has an account?" put students in a bind. Keep the talk on what they see around them and on the invented cards.

Get the numbers right.

Common Sense Media's 2026 survey found 49% of 17-year-old boys gambled in the past year, but that counts loot boxes and scratch tickets too. About 12% of all boys 11 to 17 did sports-related gambling. Avoid "half of boys bet on sports"; a student will catch it.

The law is moving.

As of fall 2026: most states with legal sportsbooks require you to be 21 (Massachusetts does). Kalshi and Polymarket take 18-year-olds nationwide under federal rules. States are suing them and federal courts disagree, so if students ask, say it's being fought out in court right now.

Watch for chasing.

Talk of winning money back, borrowing or taking money, using a parent's card or a relative's account, or betting to feel better are worth a quiet check-in after advisory and a same-day note to a counselor. No screening questions in the group.

Some students are hurting from someone else's betting.

A parent's or sibling's gambling can mean money trouble and tension at home. If a student goes quiet or mentions it, follow up privately and connect them with a counselor.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Families and cultures differ.

March Madness pools, poker night, mahjong, dominoes, the lottery, raffles: gambling is part of family life in many homes, and forbidden in others for religious reasons. Present facts about the apps, not judgments about anyone's family.

Money looks different from seat to seat.

A $50 loss is pocket change for one student and a week's groceries for another. Keep examples to the math, avoid assumptions about spending money, and never make a student's own money part of the activity.

Not every student follows sports.

Some students don't watch sports at all. The coin flips need no sports knowledge, and the cards include esports and gaming. Students who play games with loot boxes or skins will recognize the same pull.

Girls and nonbinary students bet too.

Most of the research is on boys, and the apps market to young men. Use varied names on the cards and avoid framing this as a guy problem; anyone can get pulled in, and anyone can be the friend who notices.

Neurodivergent students.

Students with ADHD may feel the pull of fast, rewarding apps more strongly. Keep that matter-of-fact and private. Concrete math and cards work better than abstract talk about risk.

Language.

Betting has its own vocabulary (parlay, prop, spread, odds). Define each word as it comes up, and let English learners answer with a number, a gesture, or a word in any language.

What the research says

36% of US boys age 11 to 17 gambled in the past year, rising from 32% at 11 to 49% at 17. That includes loot boxes, skins, cards with friends and scratch tickets. 12% of all boys did sports-related gambling, and 60% of those do it at least monthly.

Common Sense Media, Betting on Boys, 2026 (survey of 1,017 boys, July 2025)

Friends matter most: 84% of boys whose friends mostly gamble also gamble, compared with 17% of boys with no gambling friends. A third (34%) have gambled with family, and only 45% say their family has rules about gambling.

Common Sense Media, 2026

Boys who lost $51 or more were nearly three times as likely to use a parent's card without permission (21% vs 8%), and half (49%) spent more than they planned.

Common Sense Media, 2026

83% of teachers surveyed had seen or heard of students gambling; sports betting was the most common form. Rates didn't differ between states with and without legal betting.

Next Gen Personal Finance flash survey, April 2026

Young males, youth who start with online sports betting, youth with depression, anxiety or substance use, and youth whose parents gamble are more likely to develop gambling problems. An early big win is a known predictor.

National Council on Problem Gambling, Youth Gambling Factsheet, 2025

Ordinary Kalshi users lost an estimated $583.5 million from July 2021 to May 2026, $371.6 million of it on sports. On Polymarket, the top 1% of profitable users captured 76.5% of the profits.

Roosevelt Institute, 2026; Akey, Grégoire, Harvie & Martineau, CEPR Discussion Paper 21615, 2026

Where online sports betting became legal, bankruptcies rose, with the biggest effects among young men in lower-income areas. Another analysis disputes the bankruptcy finding.

Hollenbeck, Larsen & Proserpio, Management Science (SSRN 4903302); Progressive Policy Institute, 2025

Among men 18 to 25, more frequent sports betting predicted more severe problem gambling.

Mancini et al., Journal of Gambling Studies, 2025
